source_policy: Regional 1999 Flora for its direct descriptions; Kew POWO/GrassBase for modern taxonomy and taxa not treated in the regional flora; 2015 Hill Country key for historical region-name context. Previously saved Hays source photo inspection is reused only. Unknown not absent.
deliberate_holds: Paspalum notatum turf/pasture vs established roadside occurrence
Oplismenus hirtellus historical setarius species concept and uncertain groundcover establishment
Sphenopholis interrupta under historic Trisetum interruptum name
Hordeum murinum old leporinum subspecies treatment
Rostraria cristata no direct species treatment in regional Flora

flora_source.citation: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, Poaceae
flora_source.applicability: 1999 Flora species treatment and Kew POWO/GrassBase; old variety key conflicting with the broad species branch-count summary must not be promoted as diagnosis

source_backed_character_targets.description: Mat-forming rhizomatous perennial, with flowering culms typically about 20–75 cm in the regional Flora
Usually two nearly paired racemes at the summit, occasionally a third; each roughly 4–12(–15) cm in the Flora
Broadly ovate to obovate glabrous spikelets, usually 2.5–3.8 mm across modern treatments
Spikelets single and arranged in two rows along the raceme axis
Lower glume typically absent or poorly developed, upper glume smooth and about as long as the spikelet
Short ligule with hairs described in POWO accounts; examine exact collar rather than inferring from turf

taxa.previously_seen_hays_photo_features: Clearly forked Y/V-shaped pair of spike-like racemes with small spikelets; smooth narrow leaves and mowed lawn/field context.
taxa.not_seen_hays_photo_features: Paired racemes strongly support Bahia grass but microscopic broadly ovate glumes and seed size not confirmed; many records from lawns and could be introduced turf.
taxa.comparator_species: Paspalum distichum, P. dilatatum, P. pubiflorum, other paired-raceme Paspalum
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: Measure and dissect a mature isolated spikelet and verify rhizome/base, true ligule and branch orientation on the same Hays plant; separate mowed planted turf from naturalized colonies.
taxa.caution: Several Hays observations are mowed lawns. Two forked racemes alone do not establish wild Hays occurrence. The regional Flora's infraspecific branch counts are inconsistent with its species-level generalization; do not use varietal thresholds without a modern key.

flora_source.citation: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, Poaceae
flora_source.applicability: 1999 Flora explicit species and brome couplet; Kew POWO modern detailed species morphology

source_backed_character_targets.description: Introduced cool-season annual with often soft-hairy lower sheaths
Open or nodding panicle with drooping branches, not a unique species-level character
Old regional Bromus key gives about 12–18 mm awns, while broader Kew treatment gives 10–25 mm; use source-specific ranges
Very elongated thin transparent apical lemma teeth, about 2–5 mm under regional key
Membranous ligule approximately 2–5 mm, margin often torn
Lemma may be hairy or nearly hairless under varieties described in the regional Flora

taxa.previously_seen_hays_photo_features: Two observations display open, drooping, long-awned brome panicles.
taxa.not_seen_hays_photo_features: Unmeasured lemma awns and sheaths do not distinguish cheatgrass reliably from other annual brome species; just 2 local records.
taxa.comparator_species: Bromus japonicus, B. secalinus, B. hordeaceus, B. catharticus
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: Detach mature lemma and show long apical teeth plus distinct long awn and glume/lemma nervation with mm scale; verify basal sheath hairs on the same plant.
taxa.caution: Only two previously reviewed Hays images and no measured lemma-apex teeth. Do not infer cheatgrass merely from drooping long-awned brome heads.

flora_source.citation: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, Poaceae
flora_source.applicability: Direct 1999 Flora under Trisetum interruptum with explicit Sphenopholis interrupta alternate classification; POWO accepted Sphenopholis genus placement

source_backed_character_targets.description: Annual grass roughly 7–50(–60) cm tall, leaf sheaths pubescent
Asymmetrical membranous ligule 1.5–2 mm with irregular ragged margin
Narrow spike-like panicle, which can appear interrupted
Spikelets 2–3-flowered, around 4–6 mm excluding the awns
Lemma with two slender apical teeth
Awn arising on back near base of apical teeth, twisted and bent, about 5–8 mm

taxa.previously_seen_hays_photo_features: Slender interrupted-looking spikes with close-up overlapping green spikelets and sheath/stem junction views.
taxa.not_seen_hays_photo_features: Second glume shape, ligule and floret details not decisively visible; compare existing Sphenopholis obtusata candidate.
taxa.comparator_species: Sphenopholis obtusata, Koeleria macrantha, Rostraria cristata
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: Separate mature spikelets to count florets, backlight the lemma's two teeth and precisely show the insertion of its twisted awn; obtain true ligule macro and compare with S. obtusata.
taxa.caution: Interrupted-looking flowering heads are not species-specific; the old Trisetum genus label is a nomenclatural alias, not an extra candidate.

flora_source.citation: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, Poaceae
flora_source.treatment_name: No direct named treatment in 1999 Flora
flora_source.applicability: Species-rank diagnosis comes from Kew POWO/GrassBase and Flora of Oman, not from 1999 Flora

source_backed_character_targets.description: Small tufted annual, culms generally 5–45 cm in GrassBase
Membranous ligule about 1 mm, lacking long hair fringe
Narrow dense to interrupted spike-like panicle approximately 1.5–10 cm in GrassBase
Spikelets approximately 3–7 mm and typically 3–8 fertile florets
Lower glume often 1-veined and shorter, upper glume around 3-veined and broader
Lemma awn may be apical/subapical and short, approximately 0–3 mm

taxa.previously_seen_hays_photo_features: Short cylindrical green bristly panicle with densely overlapping awned or pointed spikelets; small tufted grass.
taxa.not_seen_hays_photo_features: Actual glume and lemma awn origins, floret counts and ligule unclear; compact spikelike heads resemble other small pooid grasses.
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: Isolate several ripe florets and both glumes with a 1-mm scale, photograph awn origin, floret count and true ligule; compare with similar dense-headed annual Pooideae.
taxa.caution: Compact green bristly heads are not species proof. The 1999 regional Flora has no direct Rostraria cristata species treatment.

flora_source.citation: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, Poaceae
flora_source.treatment_name: Polypogon viridis (Flora 1999; historical Agrostis semiverticillata alias)
flora_source.applicability: Direct Flora species treatment; Kew POWO/GrassBase modern confirmation. Glume-awn absence separates from bristly P. monspeliensis.

source_backed_character_targets.description: Glabrous grass with bent/decumbent stem base, often in wet creek and spring habitats; Flora culms about 15–45(–70) cm
Membranous ligule approximately 2–7 mm in regional Flora (other treatments may give shorter values)
Condensed panicle roughly 4–12 cm long and 1–3 cm broad in regional Flora
Small spikelets about 1.3–2(–2.5) mm in the Flora
Glumes and lemmas typically awnless; unlike rabbitfoot P. monspeliensis with long glume awns
Glumes lightly roughened, one-veined, broad near apex in GrassBase account

taxa.previously_seen_hays_photo_features: Moist rock/creek-edge habitat and narrow, somewhat contracted flowering panicles.
taxa.not_seen_hays_photo_features: Awnless spikelet structure and ligule length not distinguished from other bentgrasses.
taxa.comparator_species: Polypogon monspeliensis, Agrostis spp., other wet meadow bentgrasses
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: Photograph a complete creekside Hays specimen with measured ligule and detached awnless spikelets, then compare with bristle-awned P. monspeliensis.
taxa.caution: Wetland setting and a narrow panicle alone cannot distinguish this taxon; old Agrostis combination should be kept searchable.

flora_source.citation: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, Poaceae
flora_source.applicability: Flora 1999 treats subsp. leporinum; Kew accepts murinum species and several subspecies—do not assign subspecies from unmeasured Hays photos

source_backed_character_targets.description: Annual hare barley, generally 30–75 cm in older regional subsp. leporinum account
Barley-like spike of groups of three spikelets at successive joints, central fertile with lateral companions
Glumes of central spikelet have hairs/ciliate margins in regional key
Leaf sheath auricles present; distinguish from H. pusillum lacking auricles in regional key
Lemma awns in the leporinum account typically around 10–35 mm
Regional group key mentions slender lemmas 1.3–1.9 mm wide and leaf blades 1–6 mm

taxa.previously_seen_hays_photo_features: Short dense barley-like awned heads and annual bunches shown.
taxa.not_seen_hays_photo_features: Glume/ciliate margins and hybrid/subspecies-level distinctions not observed; older Flora treats subsp. leporinum.
taxa.comparator_species: Hordeum pusillum, H. vulgare and other wild barley grasses
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: Separate an intact three-spikelet group and photograph glume fringes, lateral pedicels and awn lengths with mm scale; record true auricles, basal habit and whether old leporinum subspecies applies.
taxa.caution: A typical awned barley head supports the genus, not murinum subspecies; the Flora's leporinum treatment cannot automatically assign modern lower-rank taxon.

flora_source.citation: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, Poaceae
flora_source.applicability: Direct Flora species; corroborated by modern Kew descriptions

source_backed_character_targets.description: Spreading annual, often roots from lower stem nodes; flowering stems commonly 10–60 cm
Short ciliate membrane usually 0.1–1 mm
Two to seven or more radiating fingerlike branches, usually around 1.5–6 cm
Flattened flowering branch has a sterile narrow tip extending about 1–7 mm beyond last spikelet
Tightly packed sessile flattened spikelets in two rows along one side of branches; about 3–4 mm
Each spikelet typically contains 3–5 florets; upper glumes and lemmas often shortly awned

taxa.previously_seen_hays_photo_features: Fingerlike branches radiating from culm apex, consistent with crowdfoot grass inflorescence.
taxa.not_seen_hays_photo_features: Images not sufficiently close to confirm branch tips projecting beyond spikelets, floret details, or rooting nodes.
taxa.comparator_species: Eleusine indica, Dactylis-like digitate grasses, Chloris species
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: Photograph sterile rachis projection beyond last mature spikelet with mm ruler, plus single detached flattened 3–5-flowered spikelet and rooted nodes.
taxa.caution: Fingerlike heads alone misclassify several Hays grasses. Needs branch-end projection and floret dissection.

flora_source.citation: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, Poaceae
flora_source.treatment_name: Oplismenus hirtellus (Flora 1999; O. setarius historical split)
flora_source.applicability: Direct Flora species account plus Kew POWO/GrassBase for modern accepted name; former O. setarius lumping is a real species-concept caution

source_backed_character_targets.description: Sprawling perennial stems root at lower nodes and form groundcover in shaded places
Broad spreading blades about 1.5–7 cm by 5–15 mm in Flora account
Short ciliate membrane at inner collar
About 3–7 short widely separated unilateral flowering branches, roughly 1–6 mm in old regional description
Spikelets in two ranks along one side; paired in modern GrassBase; two florets with fertile upper floret
Glumes awned; first glume awn typically around 5–10 mm and distinctly longer than second

taxa.previously_seen_hays_photo_features: Shaded groundcover with broad lanceolate leaf blades, sprawling stem habit and distinct long-bristled/hooked-looking spikelets in close-up.
taxa.not_seen_hays_photo_features: The precise floret/awn base and bristle count distinguishing Oplismenus species not fully resolved; no plant establishment context vetted.
taxa.comparator_species: Oplismenus undulatifolius and other creeping shade grasses, including historic O. setarius concept
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: Same Hays plant: trace rooted creeping node, show ciliate ligule and paired awned spikelets at mm scale, inspect historical setarius distinction and site planting context.
taxa.caution: Flora treats O. setarius broadly within hirtellus while other historical sources split it. A shaded leafy groundcover and hooked awns do not independently settle species concept or wild occurrence.
